warnings.warning: Equation 6 adds work W directly to speed squared; dimensional consistency requires the specific-work term 2W/m.
The added-force glyph collides with the curvature-radius notation and has no unambiguous definition or unit.
The printed downhill acceleration contains an extra ma factor that is dimensionally incompatible with dv_x/dt and absent from code.
The second if branch overwrites left-wall curvature and leaves the flat-region slope unassigned.
The right branch overwrites the computed slope with 0.5 and fails to assign the second derivative.
The derivative map uses Y5 and the time-loop guard uses Y4 before either state is initialized; the declared pumping parameter is not present in the state derivative.
The appendix restores force-level mass factors, whereas the body uses acceleration-level N; future writing must provide an explicit symbol and unit crosswalk.

global_organization_chain: Open by opposing the single mathematical objective of vertical air with cycles, stunt launch, and practical-course criteria.
Narrow the sport history to the literal half-pipe and define vertical air before introducing any equation.
Decompose the facility into vertical, transition, and flat, then map each component to gravity, balance, pumping, landing, and recovery.
Convert the domain questions into a named three-rung model ladder: energy baseline, two-dimensional force ODE, and three-dimensional slope extension.
Within every model rung, repeat the visible sequence How It Works -> equations and figure -> Consequences -> Strengths -> Weaknesses, so each omission motivates the next rung.
Mirror the same energy -> 2D -> 3D order in Results, while moving from analytic limits to component tables and trajectory figures.
Synthesize the maximum recommendation by walking through all three model rungs, then reopen the decision under a practical rider scenario.
Separate physical analogy, computational invariants, nested-model recovery, analytical limits, and numerical error claims into a dedicated testing section.
Translate remaining geometry, active-work, and rider-control omissions into future work rather than hiding them inside the recommendation.
Close the evidence trail with seven appendix pages of parameters, derivative code, RK4 updates, geometry figures, scenario tables, and an equation recap, followed by source families.

main_argument_chains.claim: Vertical air depends first on available energy and takeoff direction, so the energy model supplies a limiting baseline rather than the final design.
support_steps: Mechanical-energy conservation reduces to speed from the release-height difference under zero initial speed.
The no-work case cannot exceed the release height, which exposes the need for athlete work.
The takeoff-angle limits separate horizontal from vertical velocity.
main_argument_chains.decision_consequence: Use the energy branch to check passive limits and motivate pumping; do not use it alone to select practical geometry.

main_argument_chains.claim: Cross-sectional geometry is intended to affect exit response through slope, curvature-dependent normal loading, friction, drag, and active work.
support_steps: A replaceable z(y) interface links each candidate profile to local angle and curvature.
Equations 7-10 resolve drag, normal loading, friction, and the added-force proxy into y-z accelerations.
Runge-Kutta integration is intended to produce comparable paths and exit components.
Matched no-work and added-work figures make the mechanism comparison visible.
main_argument_chains.decision_consequence: Retain the geometry-to-force-to-output organization, but make future rankings conditional on matched depth, width, endpoint angle, and event definitions.

main_argument_chains.claim: Adding hill slope expands the design space from cross-section alone to shape-slope pairs.
support_steps: Figure 3 rotates the coordinate frame so hill angle phi enters gravity components.
Equations 11-13 add downhill velocity while retaining the y-z force balance.
The results repeat the same candidate comparison at selected slope settings and expose x, y, and z motion visually.
main_argument_chains.decision_consequence: Treat the 45-degree Parabola 1 result as a conditional component-velocity ranking until world-vertical flight distance, landing, and coupled vector losses are computed.

main_argument_chains.claim: The paper distinguishes a tested maximum from a practical recommendation by changing the behavioral scenario.
support_steps: The solution section first triangulates a near-vertical takeoff, Parabola 1, and a 45-degree mountain slope.
It then names unmodeled carving and directional velocity conversion as limits.
The practical branch keeps Parabola 1 and changes the hill slope to 25 degrees.
main_argument_chains.decision_consequence: Preserve the maximum-to-practical pivot as an organizational pattern, but require explicit safety, landing, cycle, construction, and rider-control criteria before calling the variant practical.

main_argument_chains.claim: Credibility is organized through multiple distinct checks rather than one undifferentiated validation claim.
support_steps: A physical marble analogue is paired with a simulated 3D trajectory.
Removing losses and work targets conservative and damped limiting behavior.
Setting phi=0 targets nested recovery of the 2D model.
The energy invariant and time-step claim address analytical and numerical questions separately.
The full code appendix makes the implementation inspectable.
main_argument_chains.decision_consequence: Keep this physical-computational-analytical sequence, while labeling the marble comparison illustrative and requiring executable assertions, convergence grids, and residuals for validation.

visualization_dispositions.analytical_purpose: A simple energy diagram makes release height, coping height, speed, and angle intuitive.
The force overlay connects normal, gravity, and tangent motion to a real half-pipe profile.
A rotated-axis diagram clarifies the intended three-dimensional extension.
Before-and-after work trajectory plots are easy to compare but lack constraint residuals and unit-complete legends.
The three-dimensional path communicates downhill cycles but is difficult to read quantitatively.
The apparatus and simulation pairing is persuasive visually but has no registered overlay or residual.
Color-coded scenario tables are scannable but mix cycle events and unexplained zeros.
The compact result table omits cycle alignment, x speed, uncertainty, and scalar objective.
